doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Freddie Green, Basie rhythm guitar and Herb Ellis
summary: Discussion of Freddie Green's playing, the Basie band guitar, the amp anecdote from Bill Crow, and Herb Ellis.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Think if Freddie Green had a penny for every chomp he did.
Oh wow. He was fabulous. The guitar would be like this, did you ever see the way he played? That’s why he was playing on the bottom string.
Okay.
If you notice, you see instead of like this he was hitting them like this.
See I thought it was the top strings more. I knew he didn’t play all the strings.
Well you know, the lower.
The lower strings. So on the other fingers he would sort of just deaden the other strings or you just don’t hit them?

You can deaden them. You deaden them. But it gives you that nice — without that with Basie, I mean no one can beat Freddie Green on that. But now that’s a different — when you get a chance listen to Basie, then listen to Johnny Mathis with Tony. It’s a little different. Tony’s was more, you can hear the change more. And it’s just fabulous with Tony. I think he used an L5 I’m pretty sure, where on Basie, I think he used a Gretsch, I think he played a Gretsch guitar, a big body Gretsch.

There’s a little anecdote about him when he had an amp for a while and he would want to take solos but the guys in the band kept sabotaging the amp. Because when he stopped © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
playing rhythm the band fell apart. So for the sake of the band the guys kept disconnecting the speakers.
I never heard that.
Yeah I read that in that Bill Crow. Have you ever seen that Bill Crow Jazz Anecdotes? Oh you’d get a big kick out of that.
Oh all right. I’ll have to write that down.
Yeah it’s got these little stories.
That’s cute, wow. Because I was wondering if he could, he probably could.
He probably could have. I have one CD with him and Herb Ellis called “Rhythm Willie” where he plays a little bit. It’s pretty nice.
Oh. With Herb. Okay.
He definitely, that was his thing. His stock in trade.
I haven’t seen Herb Ellis in many, many years.
Yeah. He’s still around.

He’s still around, God bless him. He was at Fat Tuesday’s when we were there and that was in the eighties, yes in the eighties was the last time I saw him. He was the highest paid jazz guitarist on recording, I guess you know that, right?
I didn’t know that.

Oh yeah at one point in eighty — I can’t remember, in eighty-something. It was right in the magazines, who was paid the highest in what categories: rock, jazz. And Herb Ellis was on more jazz records, and wow.
